references.text: Both verses describe that the priest shall take a portion of the memorial offering (אַזְכָּרָה) and burn it on the altar as a fire offering to the Lord.
The priest burns the portion of the memorial offering on the altar as a fire offering to the Lord, the same practice as in verse 9.
Describes the burnt offering as a pleasing aroma (רֵיחַ נִיחֹחַ) to the Lord, the same expression used for the grain offering.
The offering is burned on the altar as a pleasing aroma to the Lord, the same theological concept of a fragrant scent.
A fire offering with a pleasing aroma to the Lord (אִשֵּׁה רֵיחַ נִיחֹחַ לַיהוָה), identical wording.
Provides further instructions about the grain offering and the portion of the memorial offering that is burned on the altar.
The burnt offering as a pleasing aroma (רֵיחַ נִיחֹחַ) and fire offering to the Lord, the same terminology.
The Lord smelled the soothing aroma (רֵיחַ הַנִּיחֹחַ), the first occurrence of this expression in Scripture.
A drink offering as a pleasing aroma to the Lord, part of the same sacrificial system.
Paul uses Old Testament language about a fragrant offering (ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας) to describe Christ's self-sacrifice.
The gifts from the Philippians are described as a fragrant offering (ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας), pleasing to God.
Theological parallel: Confirms that the principle of the 'memorial offering' (a handful plus burning) also applies within the context of the sin offering.
